title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 29
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Writing Down a Language
passages.text:
A. The earliest word lists were not dictionaries in any modern sense. They were aids for reading difficult texts — glossaries of hard words, foreign terms and technical vocabulary — and they assumed a reader who already knew the language and needed help only at its edges. Ordinary words were omitted because nobody imagined a use for defining them.

B. The shift to recording a whole language brought a problem that has never been solved and can only be managed. A language has no boundary: new words appear continuously, old ones persist in some communities and not others, and the decision about what belongs is a judgement rather than an observation. Every dictionary is therefore a selection presented as a description, and the selection reflects who compiled it.

C. Authority became attached to these books in a way their compilers did not always intend. Users treated a word's presence as permission and its absence as prohibition, and asked of a dictionary a question it was not designed to answer: not what a word means but whether it is allowed. Some compilers accepted the role; others protested that they were recording usage rather than licensing it, and lost the argument with their readers.

D. Citation evidence transformed the work from opinion into something closer to measurement. Collecting real examples of a word in use, dated and attributed, allowed a definition to be derived from evidence rather than asserted, and allowed the history of a meaning to be traced. The method required enormous quantities of reading, was carried out largely by unpaid volunteers, and took decades longer than anyone estimated.

E. The digital corpus changed the scale and the questions that could be asked. Where a compiler once had whatever citations volunteers happened to send, a searchable body of millions of texts shows how often a word occurs, in what contexts, with what other words, and how those patterns shift over time. Frequency became measurable, and definitions could be written around what is typical rather than around what a compiler had noticed.

F. What has not changed is the underlying judgement, and the technology has partly obscured that. A corpus reports what was written by whoever produced the texts in it, so a body of published writing under-represents speech, informal registers and communities that publish less, and a definition derived from it inherits those absences. The measurement is real and the selection preceding it remains a decision made by people.

passages.title: Why the Brain Keeps Time
passages.text:
Music engages more of the brain simultaneously than almost anything else people do, and the reason is that it is not one activity. Pitch, rhythm, timbre, emotional response, movement and memory are handled by different systems that happen to be coordinated by the experience, which is why damage can remove one component while leaving the others intact — a person may lose the ability to recognise a melody while still responding to rhythm, or the reverse.

Rhythm has a stronger claim to being fundamental than melody does. Humans synchronise movement to a beat spontaneously and from early childhood, and the ability is rare in other species — largely confined to some birds and mammals capable of vocal learning, which is a suggestive association rather than an explanation. Coordinating movement to an external pulse is the part of musical behaviour that looks least like a cultural accident.

Expectation is what generates the emotional effect, on the account with the strongest support. Music sets up patterns, and the listener's brain continuously predicts what comes next; satisfying that prediction, delaying it, or breaking it produces the responses that listeners describe as tension and release. This explains why familiarity increases rather than reduces enjoyment for most listeners, and why music from an unfamiliar tradition can be hard to feel anything about — the predictions have not been learned.

The therapeutic claims divide sharply by how specific they are. That rhythmic cueing improves walking in some movement disorders is well supported, with a plausible mechanism in the coupling between auditory and motor systems. That music aids memory retrieval in some forms of dementia is supported by consistent observation, though the mechanism is less clear. Broader claims — that musical training raises general intelligence, or that passive listening improves reasoning — have not survived attempts to replicate them.

Training does change the brain measurably, and the interpretation requires care. Musicians show structural and functional differences in auditory and motor regions, and the differences are larger for those who began earlier and practised more. Whether training produced the differences or people with those differences persisted at training is not fully separable without following people from before they start, and the studies that have done so find real but considerably more modest effects than the correlational literature implies.

What survives all the deflation is unusual enough to state plainly. An activity with no evident survival function, present in every known human society, engaging systems built for other purposes, and capable of coordinating the behaviour and emotional state of large groups of people simultaneously, is not adequately explained by any current account. That is a reasonable place for a field to be, and a poor reason to accept explanations that overreach.

passages.title: The Business of Empty Seats
passages.text:
An airline sells a product that cannot be stored, and every consequence of its strange economics follows from that. A seat on a departed flight is not inventory that can be sold tomorrow; it is revenue that has permanently disappeared. Meanwhile almost all the cost of operating that flight — aircraft, crew, fuel, landing charges — is incurred whether the seat is occupied or not, so the marginal cost of carrying one more passenger is very small and the marginal revenue from selling one more seat is nearly all profit.

This structure produces the pricing that passengers find arbitrary and that is in fact the only rational response to it. If a departing seat is worthless, any price above the trivial cost of carrying the passenger is better than nothing, and an airline that refused to discount would fly emptier at higher fares and earn less. The same seat therefore sells at many prices depending on when it was bought, how full the flight is, and what the buyer is estimated to be willing to pay.

Competition in this industry has been unusually destructive to its own participants. Low marginal costs mean that any carrier with unsold seats has an incentive to cut prices, which every competitor matches, and the resulting fares can cover marginal costs while failing to cover the fixed ones for years at a time. The cumulative profit of the industry over its history is close to zero and has been negative in several decades, which is remarkable for a service that has grown continuously.

Network structure is the main defence against that arithmetic. Routing traffic through a hub allows an airline to fill aircraft on routes that could not support direct service, since passengers travelling to many destinations share the same first flight. It also concentrates delay, since a disruption at the hub propagates through the network, and it creates a position on connecting routes that is difficult for a new entrant to attack without building a comparable network.

The low-cost model succeeded by removing the network rather than by cutting service. Flying point to point with a single aircraft type, from cheaper secondary airports, with fast turnarounds and no connecting obligations, produced a cost per seat that established carriers could not match without dismantling the structure that was their main asset. The saving came from operational simplicity far more than from the charges for luggage and refreshments that passengers notice.

Environmental constraint is the change the industry's economics are least equipped for. Aviation is difficult to decarbonise because the energy density of liquid fuel is not readily matched, alternatives are expensive and scarce, and demand responds strongly to price in an industry whose long-run margins are already negligible. A sector that has never reliably earned its cost of capital is being asked to fund a technological transition, which is a harder problem than the engineering one.
